deck: 30 Thinking in Java::22 Graphical User Interfaces

cards.front: Why was Java 1.0's AWT replaced by Swing?
cards.back: AWT looked equally mediocre everywhere and exposed only the lowest-common-denominator widgets
cards.extra: It was designed and built in a month. Swing (JFC) draws its own components, so it looks the same on every platform and offers far more widgets.
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
java.awt.Button awt = new java.awt.Button("OK");
javax.swing.JButton swing = new javax.swing.JButton("OK");
javax.swing.UIManager.setLookAndFeel("javax.swing.plaf.nimbus.NimbusLookAndFeel");
} }

cards.back: Arranges them at five regions: NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST and CENTER
cards.extra: CENTER absorbs the remaining space. Adding a second component to a region silently replaces the first, which is a common early bug.
cards.example:
javax.swing.JPanel p = new javax.swing.JPanel(new java.awt.BorderLayout());
p.add(new javax.swing.JButton("N"), java.awt.BorderLayout.NORTH);
p.add(new javax.swing.JButton("S"), java.awt.BorderLayout.SOUTH);
p.add(new javax.swing.JButton("W"), java.awt.BorderLayout.WEST); p.add(new javax.swing.JButton("E"), java.awt.BorderLayout.EAST);
p.add(new javax.swing.JLabel("C"), java.awt.BorderLayout.CENTER);

cards.back: Lays components left to right, wrapping when the row is full
cards.extra: It respects each component's preferred size, so it is the usual layout for toolbars and button rows.
cards.example:
javax.swing.JPanel panel = new javax.swing.JPanel(new java.awt.FlowLayout());
panel.add(new javax.swing.JButton("A"));
panel.add(new javax.swing.JButton("B"));

cards.back: Precise control through constraints — grid position, weight, fill, insets
cards.extra: It is the most powerful standard layout and the most verbose. The book treats it as the answer when nothing simpler fits.
cards.example:
java.awt.GridBagConstraints c = new java.awt.GridBagConstraints();
c.gridx = 0; c.gridy = 1; c.weightx = 1.0; c.fill = java.awt.GridBagConstraints.BOTH;
c.insets = new java.awt.Insets(2, 3, 4, 5);
javax.swing.JPanel p = new javax.swing.JPanel(new java.awt.GridBagLayout());
p.add(new javax.swing.JButton("A"), c);

cards.front: How does Swing deliver a button click to your code?
cards.back: Through a listener you register on the component
cards.extra: button.addActionListener(e -> ...). The event thread calls you back; the component knows nothing about your class beyond the interface.
cards.example:
javax.swing.JButton button = new javax.swing.JButton("Go");
button.addActionListener(e -> System.out.println("clicked"));
button.doClick();

cards.front: Why must GUI updates happen on the event dispatch thread?
cards.back: Swing components are not thread-safe; touching them from another thread corrupts layout and repaint
cards.extra: Use SwingUtilities.invokeLater to hand work to the EDT. Background work goes on a worker thread and reports back through it.
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() {
javax.swing.JLabel label = new javax.swing.JLabel("start");
javax.swing.SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() -> label.setText("done"));
} }
